linkages: children linked to their father and mother through the child's Social Security Number, which parents claiming a dependent-child deduction had to report on their own 1998, 1999 or 2000 tax return (possible only from 1998 onwards, and only on forms Modello Unico and 730)

separated or divorced couples retraced when both claim a positive percentage of the deduction for the same child SSN; a single 100 percent claim with no spouse information is treated as a single parent
siblings recovered by matching children whose parental record coincides on all variables in the dataset (around 171,000 parents with at least two children)
children assigned to the province of residence reported by the father (or the mother, if the father's information is missing) on the 1998 tax return
province-level mobility indices merged with ISTAT, Tuttoscuola, Guiso-Sapienza-Zingales and Guell et al. province-level indicators

sample.universe: All Italian personal income tax filers who claimed a dependent-child allowance in 1998, 1999 or 2000 for a child born between 1979 and 1983 (aged 15-19 in 1998), and those children's own 2016-2018 tax returns
sample.unit_of_observation: parent-child record (one child with their father and mother); the province is the unit for the geographic analysis
selection_rules: extract from the 1998, 1999 and 2000 tax returns all taxpayers who claim allowances for children born between 1979 and 1983 (age 15-19 in 1998)
recover, through the children's SSNs, their own tax returns for 2016, 2017 and 2018
drop observations where the age differential between mother (father) and child is above 45 (50) or below 14 years (6,658 records lost)
for the IGE, drop children with zero or negative income (about 1.6 percent)
for the PPP-adjusted analysis the sample is 1,634,970 records
for the siblings analysis, keep children aged 36 or 37 in 2017 who share an identical parental record (around 85,000 parent records)
where the Tuttoscuola school-quality indicators are used, the provincial analysis is limited to 100 provinces (Aosta, Bolzano and Trento are excluded)
sample.n_observations: 1,719,483 matched records (3,191,802 after reweighting for taxpayers who filed form 770); 110 provinces in the geographic analysis
sample.n_individuals: 1,719,483 children; 1,600,529 fathers and 1,196,230 mothers with observed income

construction_notes: income is total gross (before-tax) income; parental income is the sum of both parents' income and child income is always defined at the individual level
unless otherwise specified all incomes are nominal; 1998-2000 liras were converted to euros
both parents and children are ranked in percentiles 1-100 of their own national distribution; provincial analyses keep the national rank definitions
percentile ranks are used throughout rather than within-region ranks, so that provincial indices are comparable
AUM is computed at the national level as alpha + 25*beta = 50 - 25*beta and at the provincial level as AUM_g = alpha_g + 25*beta_g (equation 7)
the top mobility ratio is the ratio of the rank-rank slope in the top decile of the parental distribution to that in the bottom 90 percent (equation 2)
for the IGE, children with zero or negative income are dropped rather than imputed
for the attenuation/life cycle correction, log income is residualized on a quartic polynomial in age before the persistent-transitory process is estimated

the Pi indicator uses real incomes with base year 2014, and sons' income distributions in Italy and the United States are rescaled to match real income per capita growth in each country between 1999 and 2017

ICS indices are built on last names with fewer than 15, 20, 25 and 30 individuals per province; the three officially bilingual provinces (Aosta, Bolzano, Trento) are excluded from the ICS correlations

provincial correlates are reduced to a small number of principal components per category before the multivariate analysis of Table 24: four for school quality, two for crime and one for each other category, each weighted in proportion to the variance it explains
in Tables 17-19 and 24 variables are normalized to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 so that coefficients read as correlations
the paper uses the geographic partition of Italy into 110 provinces established in 2009

links.pointer_quote: Its slope—the rank-rank slope (RRS)—is a measure of relative mobility for children with different initial conditions in terms of parental income. The estimated RRS is 0.22.

claims.statement: In the all matched parent-child pairs subsample, a one percentile increase in parental income rank is associated with a 0.220 percentile increase in the child's rank in the national child income distribution.

population.description: Matched parent-child records from Italian personal income tax returns, restricted to all matched parent-child pairs (N = 1,719,483).
population.ages: 15-19 in 1998 (parents' returns); 34-38 in 2016-2018 (children's returns), mean age 36
subgroups_defined: sons
daughters

population.selection: Children born 1979-1983 claimed as dependents, with their social security number, on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 personal income tax return for 1998, 1999 or 2000; records with a mother(father)-child age differential above 45 (50) or below 14 years were dropped (6,658 records).

identification.source_of_variation: None. The paper measures the association between parental and child income ranks in a linked administrative tax-return panel; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: A three-year average of income measured around age 36 for children and age 48 for fathers is a valid proxy for permanent (lifetime) income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: In the INPS long panel the rank correlation between a three-year average at ages 35-37 and lifetime income is 0.92, and 0.96 at ages 47-49; simulations of a persistent-transitory process (Tables 10-11) and of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model (Tables 12-13) quantify the residual attenuation and life cycle bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The matched sample is informative about the population of Italian children born 1979-1983: the match requires the child to have been claimed as a dependent on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 return, so form-770 filers (about 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low income) and non-filers (the very poor) are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Reweighting observations by the ratio of total (MU+730+770) to (MU+730) taxpayers in each income/region cell leaves the mobility estimates virtually unchanged (Table 14).

implies_edges.from: sample inclusion: child claimed as a dependent on a 1998-2000 form MU or 730 tax return

threats_discussed: attenuation bias, because the proxy for lifetime income is a three-year average and therefore measures permanent income with error
life cycle bias, because child income is observed 12 years earlier in the life cycle than the father's income
omission of taxpayers who file form 770 (around 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low-income ones), for whom no parent-child match is possible
non-filers: individuals with no income, only tax-exempt income or only small rental income file no return, so the very poor are not covered
tax evasion, whose incidence differs across income levels, occupations and areas
nominal income, while purchasing power varies substantially across Italian regions
robustness_checks: regional (Cannari and Iuzzolino 2009a) and province-level (Boeri et al. 2018) price deflators (Table 6)
simulation of a persistent-transitory income process estimated on the tax data (Tables 10-11)
simulation of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model estimated on INPS data (Tables 12-13)
reweighting for taxpayers missing because they filed form 770 (Table 14)
upward adjustment of incomes for estimated tax evasion (Table 14)
alternative definitions of parental income (father's income; top earner's income) and father-son samples in online Appendix Tables A3-A9
comparison of the administrative wage distribution with the SHIW survey (Table 2)

estimation.specification: Equation (1): OLS regression of the child's percentile rank in the national child income distribution on the parents' percentile rank in the national parental income distribution, estimated on the stated subsample. Ranks are always those of the national distribution of the core sample.

estimand.time_horizon: Child income is observed in 2016-2018, roughly 18 years after parental income in 1998-2000; fathers are observed at about age 48 and children at about age 36.

population.description: Matched parent-child records from Italian personal income tax returns, restricted to core sample with both the form-770 reweighting and the tax-evasion adjustment applied (N = 3,191,802).
population.ages: 15-19 in 1998 (parents' returns); 34-38 in 2016-2018 (children's returns), mean age 36
population.selection: Children born 1979-1983 claimed as dependents, with their social security number, on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 personal income tax return for 1998, 1999 or 2000; records with a mother(father)-child age differential above 45 (50) or below 14 years were dropped (6,658 records).

identification.source_of_variation: None. The paper measures the association between parental and child income ranks in a linked administrative tax-return panel; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: A three-year average of income measured around age 36 for children and age 48 for fathers is a valid proxy for permanent (lifetime) income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: In the INPS long panel the rank correlation between a three-year average at ages 35-37 and lifetime income is 0.92, and 0.96 at ages 47-49; simulations of a persistent-transitory process (Tables 10-11) and of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model (Tables 12-13) quantify the residual attenuation and life cycle bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The matched sample is informative about the population of Italian children born 1979-1983: the match requires the child to have been claimed as a dependent on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 return, so form-770 filers (about 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low income) and non-filers (the very poor) are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Reweighting observations by the ratio of total (MU+730+770) to (MU+730) taxpayers in each income/region cell leaves the mobility estimates virtually unchanged (Table 14).

implies_edges.from: sample inclusion: child claimed as a dependent on a 1998-2000 form MU or 730 tax return

threats_discussed: attenuation bias, because the proxy for lifetime income is a three-year average and therefore measures permanent income with error
life cycle bias, because child income is observed 12 years earlier in the life cycle than the father's income
omission of taxpayers who file form 770 (around 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low-income ones), for whom no parent-child match is possible
non-filers: individuals with no income, only tax-exempt income or only small rental income file no return, so the very poor are not covered
tax evasion, whose incidence differs across income levels, occupations and areas
nominal income, while purchasing power varies substantially across Italian regions

simulation of a persistent-transitory income process estimated on the tax data (Tables 10-11)
simulation of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model estimated on INPS data (Tables 12-13)
reweighting for taxpayers missing because they filed form 770 (Table 14)
upward adjustment of incomes for estimated tax evasion (Table 14)
alternative definitions of parental income (father's income; top earner's income) and father-son samples in online Appendix Tables A3-A9
comparison of the administrative wage distribution with the SHIW survey (Table 2)

register_source.value: Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance electronic database of Personal Income Tax returns: total gross (before-tax) individual income of the child

timing.value: Measured on the child's 2016-2018 tax returns, when children are on average 36 years old (aged 34-38).

claims.statement: Absolute upward mobility varies substantially across the 110 Italian provinces along a clear North-South gradient, with the between-macro-area component accounting for 82 percent of the total variation in AUM.

treatment.label: Macro area / province of upbringing (North versus South of Italy)

register_source.value: Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance electronic database of Personal Income Tax returns (forms Modello Unico and 730)

definition.value: The province of residence reported by the father (or mother) on the 1998 tax return, grouped into five macro areas (Northeast, Northwest, Center, South, Islands).

timing.value: Province of residence in 1998, interpreted as the area where the child grew up.

register_source.value: Derived from the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance Personal Income Tax return database

definition.value: Mean rank in the national child income distribution of children whose parents are below the median of the parental income distribution, AUM = E[R_i | R_i^P <= 50] (equation 4); computed at the national level from the rank-rank regression as alpha + 25*beta = 50 - 25*beta.

timing.value: Child income from the 2016-2018 tax returns; parental income from the 1998-2000 tax returns.

units.value: share of the cross-province variance of AUM accounted for by the between-macro-area component

magnitude.interpretation: the province with the highest AUM is Bolzano, with a value of 0.57, and the one with the lowest is Ragusa, with 0.35; the differential corresponds to nearly EUR 7,500, nearly 40 percent of median annual income in 2017

estimand.target_population: The 110 Italian provinces

population.description: Cross-section of the 110 Italian provinces of the geographic partition established in 2009; each child is assigned to the province of residence reported by her father (or her mother, if the father's information is missing) on his (her) own 1998 tax return.
population.period: mobility indices from 1998-2000 and 2016-2018 tax returns; provincial correlates from ISTAT, Tuttoscuola (2007a) and other sources in the 2000s
subgroups_defined: macro areas: Northeast, Northwest, Center, South, Islands
population.selection: Provinces are the unit of observation; the underlying microdata are the same 1,719,483 matched parent-child records used in Table 3, column 1. School-quality indicators exclude Aosta, Bolzano and Trento, limiting those analyses to 100 provinces.

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation across the 110 Italian provinces of the 2009 geographic partition, used to hold the national institutional framework fixed.

key_assumptions.assumption: The cross-province associations are not interpreted as causal: the paper states explicitly that it does not claim the correlations are causal relations.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Explicit statement opening Section VII; the analysis is presented as a guide to future research on deeper determinants.

key_assumptions.assumption: Province-level mobility indices estimated from equation (6) on the same national rank distributions are comparable across provinces, and AUM_g = alpha_g + 25*beta_g is an accurate approximation provided the rank-rank relation is linear within the province as well.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Figure 10 and online Appendix Figures A5-A6 show the rank-rank relation is close to linear at the provincial level; reweighting each parental income bin to the national share barely affects provincial mobility estimates.

key_assumptions.assumption: Each child is attributed to the province of residence her father (or mother) reported on the 1998 tax return, which is taken to be the area where the child grew up.

threats_discussed: all the socioeconomic correlates are strongly correlated with one another, so unconditional correlations cannot be attributed to any single factor
the stark North-South gradient in income levels could mechanically drive provincial differences in AUM computed on the national distribution

robustness_checks: macro area fixed effects (Northeast, Northwest, Center, South, Islands)

mobility indices computed on PPP-adjusted (regionally deflated) income
principal-component aggregation of the socioeconomic markers before the multivariate regression
unresolved_confounders: the socioeconomic markers are mutually collinear, so the conditional correlations cannot separate the deeper determinants

claims.statement: Conditional on national parental income rank and province, the parents' rank within their own provincial income distribution has no statistically significant effect on the child's national income rank.

register_source.value: Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance electronic database of Personal Income Tax returns (forms Modello Unico and 730)

definition.value: The parents' percentile rank in the income distribution of their own province, entered alongside the national parental rank and province indicators.

timing.value: Measured on the parents' 1998-2000 tax returns.

register_source.value: Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance electronic database of Personal Income Tax returns: total gross (before-tax) individual income of the child

definition.value: Percentile rank (1 to 100) of the child's own total gross income in the national distribution of child income. Child income is always defined at the individual level and taken from the 2016, 2017 and 2018 tax returns.

timing.value: Measured on the child's 2016-2018 tax returns, when children are on average 36 years old (aged 34-38).

units.value: percentile rank points of the national child income distribution per percentile point of the local parental rank

estimand.target_population: Italian children born 1979-1983 claimed as dependents on a parent's 1998-2000 personal income tax return
estimand.time_horizon: Child income is observed in 2016-2018, roughly 18 years after parental income in 1998-2000; fathers are observed at about age 48 and children at about age 36.

population.description: All matched parent-child records, with provinces assigned from the father's (or mother's) 1998 tax return.
population.ages: 15-19 in 1998 (parents' returns); 34-38 in 2016-2018 (children's returns), mean age 36
population.selection: Children born 1979-1983 claimed as dependents, with their social security number, on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 personal income tax return for 1998, 1999 or 2000; records with a mother(father)-child age differential above 45 (50) or below 14 years were dropped (6,658 records).

identification.source_of_variation: None. The paper measures the association between parental and child income ranks in a linked administrative tax-return panel; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or instrument is used.

key_assumptions.assumption: A three-year average of income measured around age 36 for children and age 48 for fathers is a valid proxy for permanent (lifetime) income.
key_assumptions.supported_by: In the INPS long panel the rank correlation between a three-year average at ages 35-37 and lifetime income is 0.92, and 0.96 at ages 47-49; simulations of a persistent-transitory process (Tables 10-11) and of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model (Tables 12-13) quantify the residual attenuation and life cycle bias.

key_assumptions.assumption: The matched sample is informative about the population of Italian children born 1979-1983: the match requires the child to have been claimed as a dependent on a parent's form Modello Unico or 730 return, so form-770 filers (about 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low income) and non-filers (the very poor) are missing.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Reweighting observations by the ratio of total (MU+730+770) to (MU+730) taxpayers in each income/region cell leaves the mobility estimates virtually unchanged (Table 14).

implies_edges.from: sample inclusion: child claimed as a dependent on a 1998-2000 form MU or 730 tax return

threats_discussed: attenuation bias, because the proxy for lifetime income is a three-year average and therefore measures permanent income with error
life cycle bias, because child income is observed 12 years earlier in the life cycle than the father's income
omission of taxpayers who file form 770 (around 25 percent of taxpayers, typically low-income ones), for whom no parent-child match is possible
non-filers: individuals with no income, only tax-exempt income or only small rental income file no return, so the very poor are not covered
tax evasion, whose incidence differs across income levels, occupations and areas
nominal income, while purchasing power varies substantially across Italian regions
robustness_checks: regional (Cannari and Iuzzolino 2009a) and province-level (Boeri et al. 2018) price deflators (Table 6)
simulation of a persistent-transitory income process estimated on the tax data (Tables 10-11)
simulation of a log-linear lifetime-earnings model estimated on INPS data (Tables 12-13)
reweighting for taxpayers missing because they filed form 770 (Table 14)
upward adjustment of incomes for estimated tax evasion (Table 14)
alternative definitions of parental income (father's income; top earner's income) and father-son samples in online Appendix Tables A3-A9
comparison of the administrative wage distribution with the SHIW survey (Table 2)
